The adaptor rows are the ones that took two attempts to measure: the first fixture put the mate twenty bases before the read, so the boundary (mateStart - 1 for a reverse-strand read) landed before every probed locus and excluded nothing while ten rows appeared to cover it. With the mate five bases into the read, p1 is missing from chr1:101 to chr1:105 and present from 106.

suites.title: AlignmentContextIteratorBuilder routing and sample order
suites.why: Two facts here reach into every locus-based tool's output and neither is visible from the builder's setters. The samples are collected with Collectors.toSet(), so LocusIteratorByState creates its per-sample managers in Java HashSet iteration order and concatenates their elements in that same order to build each pileup: the element order of a multi-sample pileup is a HashSet bucket order over the sample names, deterministic but neither sorted nor the header's. A port using a sorted map, an insertion-ordered list or a different hash would agree on single-sample data and diverge as soon as a second sample appeared, which is why java.util.HashMap's index and its order-preserving resize are ported alongside. And areIntervalsSpecified is intervals != null rather than !isEmpty(), so an empty but non-null list counts as specified, routes to IntervalOverlappingIterator, and that constructor's Utils.nonEmpty throws: an empty interval list is an error rather than an empty traversal, and only when emitEmptyLoci is off.

cases.why: From the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner. For the order half this golden is the *definition* rather than a check: the order is a java.util.HashSet's, which is GPL2 and unspecified, so the port reproduces it as an observable and the measurement wins where the two disagree. See docs/an-unspecified-order-that-reaches-the-output.md. The rows earn their place: three sample names come back in the reverse of their insertion order, five numeric names interleave as 11|1|2|3|10, and thirteen names cross the growth point. The routing half shows the empty-list asymmetry: with emitEmptyLoci off an empty non-null interval list is an IllegalArgumentException, and with it on the same list is a traversal of nothing. The contexts of every route are compared too, empty loci included: an uncovered requested locus yields a real context with an empty pileup rather than no context, and the source is advanced past rather than rewound, so a covered locus no requested interval contains is consumed and dropped.

suites.title: LocusWalker traversal
suites.why: The traversal the largest GATK archetype inherits, probed as a real LocusWalker run through the real command line so its defaults are measured rather than transcribed. Four of them are not a ReadWalker's: two default read filters rather than one, WellformedReadFilter and MappedReadFilter, so an unmapped read carrying its mate's position reaches a ReadWalker and never reaches a LocusWalker; includeDeletions true and includeNs false; emitEmptyLoci false, so an uncovered position inside -L produces no apply call at all, which a second walker subclass overriding that method measures against; and --max-depth-per-sample defaulting to 0 with a negative value being a bad argument rather than a synonym for unlimited. The fixture is ReadWalkerDump's, so a divergence between the two suites is a divergence between the traversals rather than between their inputs. The downsampling run is recorded rather than compared: the port refuses that path, and a refusal has to be measured against what the reference actually does.

cases.why: From the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner: 217 apply calls over 8 traversals. The pair that earns the suite is gap and gap-emptyloci, the same interval run both ways: six calls with the default, fifty-one with emitEmptyLoci overridden, the uncovered ones carrying a real context with zero depth and the reference base still present. One row is honest rather than covering: depth-1 produced rows identical to the undownsampled run, because this fixture never exceeds one read per sample at any locus, so it does not measure downsampling at all. The test asserts that identity so the case cannot quietly start counting as coverage, and a probe that actually downsamples belongs with the java.util.Random port the reservoir needs.

suites.title: java.util.Random sequences
suites.why: Utils.getRandomGenerator() is one static new Random(47382911L), seeded at class initialisation, so every draw in a run comes from a single stream and a consumer that takes one value too few or too many shifts that stream for every later consumer as well. The sequence therefore has to be exact before anything is allowed to draw from it, which is why this is its own slice ahead of the downsampler. Unlike HashMap's iteration order, this one is legitimately implementable from the published contract: the Javadoc states the algorithm and its constants and requires every method to produce that exact sequence. Two behaviours are probed for shape rather than value: nextInt(bound) takes a different path for a power-of-two bound, so bound 16 answers differently from what 15 and 17 would suggest, and the general path rejects biased values and redraws, so its draw count depends on the values themselves. A final interleaved sequence mixes the methods on one generator, which catches a port whose methods are individually right but whose draw counts are not.

cases.why: From the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner: 98 sequences over 7 seeds, plus 7 interleaved streams. The interleaved rows are the ones that would catch a plausible wrong port: a version whose methods are individually correct but whose draw counts are not passes every single-method row and fails those, because nextDouble and nextLong each consume two draws. The seeds include the GATK constant, zero, both extremes of long, and the multiplier itself, which scrambles to zero.

suites.title: ReservoirDownsampler selections
suites.why: Which reads a deep pileup keeps. Four behaviours change the answer without being inherent to reservoir sampling. The draw happens even when the slot is discarded: nextInt(totalReadsSeen) is called for every read past the target and only then is the slot compared against it, so a read that is thrown away still advances the shared static stream and every later draw anywhere in the run depends on how many reads were seen here. The probe therefore reports the generator's next value after each case, not only the reads kept: two cases that keep the same reads can leave the stream in different places. The bound grows with the count, so the same read draws differently depending on how many preceded it. Replacement is in place, so the reservoir's order is the order slots were last written rather than the reads' order. And setNonRandomReplacementMode swaps the draw for Math.abs(name.hashCode()) % totalReadsSeen, where Math.abs is wrong for Integer.MIN_VALUE. The generator is reset before each case, so a case measures the downsampler rather than the order the cases ran in.

cases.why: From the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner. The stream-position rows are the evidence: under-target and nonrandom both leave the generator at 1057280359, its first value, because neither took a draw, while one-over leaves it at -873351126, its second, because it took exactly one before discarding the slot. A port that skipped the draw when the slot loses would keep the same reads and fail those rows.

suites.title: Well19937c sequences
suites.why: GATK carries two static generators, not one: Utils.getRandomGenerator() is a java.util.Random and Utils.getRandomDataGenerator() is a RandomDataGenerator over a Well19937c, seeded from the same constant and reset together. They are different algorithms with different streams, and LevelingDownsampler draws from the second where ReservoirDownsampler draws from the first, so a port that routed both through one generator would agree with neither. Four shapes are probed because a port gets them wrong while looking right. The two constructors disagree: new Well19937c(long) splits the seed into two ints, high word first, so it seeds a different 624-word pool from new Well19937c((int) seed) even when the long fits in an int, and GATK uses the long one. The derived methods are not java.util.Random's: nextDouble is ((next(26) << 26) | next(26)) * 2^-52 where java.util.Random uses 27 bits and 2^-53, nextFloat takes 23 bits rather than 24, and nextLong ors its halves where java.util.Random adds them signed. nextInt(bound) is the one that does agree, because commons-math copied it from Apache Harmony, so bounds either side of 16 are dumped to confirm the power-of-two path and the rejection loop. And nextBytes takes one extra full draw after its four-at-a-time loop even when the length is a multiple of four and nothing is left to fill, so lengths 0 through 9 are dumped with the generator's next value after each. nextGaussian is deliberately absent from both the dump and the port: it goes through commons-math's own FastMath, whose cos, sin, log and sqrt are its implementations rather than the platform's, so a port of its shape would be bit-wrong in the mantissa while looking right. It belongs with jmath.

cases.why: From the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner. The rows that matter most are the interleaved ones and the nextBytes rows: the first catch a port whose methods are individually right but whose draw counts are not, and the second catch the unconditional trailing draw, which is invisible in the bytes themselves and visible only in where the stream ends up.

suites.title: LevelingDownsampler and the permutation underneath it
suites.why: LevelingDownsampler cuts several stacks down to one total, and it removes items through MathUtils.sampleIndicesWithoutReplacement, which is RandomDataGenerator.nextPermutation over the static Well19937c. Both layers decide the answer, so both are dumped. nextPermutation(n, k) shuffles all n entries and returns the first k, so it costs n - 1 draws whatever k is: sampling 2 of 1000 spends 999 draws and moves the stream for every later consumer, which is why the probe reports the generator's next value after each call. Its shuffle runs downwards with shrinking bounds, and its last step takes no draw at all, so the cost is n - 1 rather than n. The indices it returns are the shuffled head and are therefore unsorted, and since the caller uses them only as membership, the raw list is dumped so that a port which sorted them still fails. Above that, the leveling plan is pure arithmetic: a round-robin walk over the sizes decrements one at a time, so how many go from each stack is fixed before any draw and only which ones is random. The walk stops on consecutive refusals rather than on a scan. A stack that keeps everything takes no draw, so stack sizes shift the stream for the stacks after them. LinkedList and ArrayList take different removal paths upstream and must keep the same items, so both are dumped and a divergence between them is a failure rather than an assumption. And with minElementsPerStack of zero a stack can be planned down to nothing, at which point nextPermutation throws NotStrictlyPositiveException instead of returning an empty selection.

cases.why: From the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner. The stream-position rows are the evidence for the draw counts, and the target-zero pair is the evidence for the refusal: with minElementsPerStack one the stacks fall to one item each, and with zero the same target reaches nextPermutation(n, 0) and throws.

suites.title: VariantWalker traversal
suites.why: The traversal every variant-based tool inherits, run through the real command line rather than reconstructed. Reading FeatureIntervalIterator suggests that -L can produce duplicates: featureIsNovel tests a feature against previousInterval alone, one interval of memory rather than a set, so a variant covered by intervals 1 and 3 but not by 2 would reach apply twice. The suite measures that and the answer is no: three intervals whose first and third are identical produce two apply calls rather than four, and intervals given out of order are traversed in sorted order. The argument layer sorts and merges before the traversal sees the list, so the precondition the iterator documents is always satisfied through a command line. The behaviour is real in the class and unreachable in the tool, which is a different claim from saying it does not happen, and the distinction is exactly what a golden is for. And an empty interval list is not an empty traversal: setIntervalsForTraversal maps both null and an empty list to null, which means no restriction at all. The record fields travel with each apply call because the walker is also where a decoded record becomes what a tool sees: the interval it builds is SimpleInterval(variant), whose end is the END attribute when the record carries one and start plus the reference allele's length minus one otherwise.

suites.title: Where an assembly region starts and stops
suites.why: The boundaries HaplotypeCaller and Mutect2 assemble over: a boundary that moves by one base changes the haplotypes and therefore the calls, so this is upstream of every variant those tools emit. Four behaviours decide it and none follows from cutting where the activity changes. A probability is spread over a Gaussian and the spread is added rather than assigned, so the probability at a site is the sum of its neighbours' tails and a site never reported active can cross the threshold, while a probability of exactly zero skips the filter entirely. The filter width is chosen from the kernel's values rather than from sigma, and it feeds back into getMaxProbPropagationDistance, which decides when a region may be popped at all. The cut site is a local minimum searched backwards, and isMinimum is asymmetric, requiring p[i] <= p[i+1] but p[i] < p[i-1], so a plateau is cut at its left-hand end. And nothing may be popped until the profile holds maxRegionSize plus the propagation distance in states, so regions appear in bursts rather than as soon as their activity ends. The kernels are compared as raw bits because the last bits are the point: Math.exp is the platform's and a port whose exp differs in the final ulp moves a cut site.

suites.title: The assembly region itself: spans, reads, trimming
suites.why: What HaplotypeCaller and Mutect2 actually assemble, once the activity profile has decided where a region starts and stops: a primary span for calling, a padded span for assembly, and the reads overlapping the padded one. Four behaviours are measured because none is what the class says. The padding constructor goes through IntervalUtils.trimIntervalToContig, which returns null rather than throwing when the padded interval cannot be placed on the contig, and the null then reaches Utils.nonNull inside the other constructor, so the failure is reported as a null padded span and never mentions padding. trim(span, padding) does not produce the region its own javadoc describes: the javadoc works an example, active 100-200 padded 50-250 trimmed to 150-225 giving a region 150-200 with 25bp of padding, but the code expands the requested span by the requested padding and intersects that with the old padded span, so the padding is never recomputed to fit. Trimming re-clips every read to the new padded span, drops the ones left empty or no longer overlapping, and then sorts the survivors with ReadCoordinateComparator, so the read order of a trimmed region is not the order the reads were added in and the comparator is observable output rather than an internal detail. And trimming drops the hard-clipped pileup reads entirely, because the new region is constructed empty and only addAll is called on it. The comparator is dumped over every ordered pair of the corpus, so its antisymmetry is measured too: a comparator that is not antisymmetric sorts differently under a different sort algorithm.

suites.title: The iterators between a shard of reads and an activity profile
suites.why: LocusIteratorByState yields nothing at all for a locus no read covers, so a position with zero depth is silently absent from its output. The assembly-region traversal cannot work that way, because the activity profile has to see the gap in order to close a region over it, and AssemblyRegionIterator therefore wraps the locus iterator in IntervalAlignmentContextIterator, whose whole job is to walk every base of every interval and manufacture an empty AlignmentContext wherever the wrapped iterator has none. The comment upstream is unusually direct about the stakes: this is critical for reproducing GATK 3.x behavior. A port that skipped the wrapper would produce regions ending at the last covered base instead of where the activity dies, which moves every boundary downstream of a coverage gap. Underneath it, ShardedIntervalIterator computes shard indices over the interval length and converts them back to coordinates, so the arithmetic is absolute rather than relative and the last shard is truncated against the interval end; IntervalLocusIterator is that class at shard size 1. The corpus has deliberate gaps before, inside and after its reads, and the intervals asked for start before the coverage, end after it, sit entirely inside a gap, and cross a contig boundary.

suites.title: The assembly-region traversal: loci in, regions out
suites.why: Where the activity profile, the assembly region and the locus iterators meet, and what HaplotypeCaller and Mutect2 are once the assembler is removed: a region boundary that moves by one base here changes their calls. Four behaviours are measured and three are invisible from any tool output. A shard carries two interval lists built the same way, the padded one with the padding and the unpadded one with zero, and passing zero is not a no-op because getIntervalsWithFlanks sorts and merges with IntervalMergingRule.ALL whatever the padding is, so the reads are queried over one list while the loci are walked over another. The profile is popped before the current pileup is added and the force flag is that this locus does not continue the profile, which the upstream comment insists on: adding first would make the profile contiguous with the new pileup, the force would never fire, and a region would never be closed at a gap between two intervals. A region popped from the profile is not ready, but waits in a queue until the loci have advanced past the end of its padded span, because until then the reads that belong in it have not been read. And reads are carried forward from the previous region as well as taken from the cache, so a read spanning a boundary is in both regions, while a read is left in the cache only when its start is past the region padded end. The evaluator is a probe rather than a caller, activity being a declared function of pileup depth, so the regions are decided by the traversal and not by anything statistical.

suites.title: What an AssemblyRegionWalker hands to apply()
suites.why: The last of the five walker archetypes and the one HaplotypeCaller and Mutect2 are built on. The probe is a real AssemblyRegionWalker run through the real command line rather than a reconstruction, so its defaults are measured rather than transcribed: min 50, max 300, padding 100, threshold 0.002, propagation 50, from an argument collection the walker instantiates without overriding anything. Four behaviours are the point and three are invisible from any tool output. There is one read shard per contig rather than one per interval, so two -L arguments on the same contig share a shard and an activity profile and can end up in one region if the padding joins them, while two on different contigs cannot whatever their distance. apply receives its reference and feature contexts over the region padded span rather than its active span, so a tool reads bases outside the territory it may call in, which is the point of the padding. force-active rewrites isActive after the iterator has produced the region, so it marks every region active without moving a single boundary, where a port folding it into the evaluator would return one enormous region instead. And the default read filters are WellformedReadFilter and MappedReadFilter, the same pair as a LocusWalker and not a ReadWalker single filter, so an unmapped read parked at its mate coordinate never reaches this traversal. The fixture is the read walker one, so a divergence between these suites is a divergence between traversals rather than between inputs.

suites.title: The rank-sum test
suites.why: MannWhitneyU is the test behind BaseQRankSum, MQRankSum, ReadPosRankSum and ClippingRankSum, and four of its decisions are not what a rank-sum test suggests. The ranks are floats: the values are doubles while the ranks, their sums and the averaged rank of a tie band are all single precision, so a port that ranked in double precision would agree on small inputs and drift on realistic ones. Two different tests are chosen by size, with either series at ten or more taking the normal approximation and anything smaller enumerating every permutation of the group labels, so the reported Z comes from a cumulative probability in one regime and from an inverse cumulative probability in the other, and commons-math3's two are not inverses of each other. transformTies reports zero ties when every single value is tied, because the sigma formula breaks down there, and the continuity correction is then dropped as well, so two mechanisms conspire to produce exactly one half. And the permutation p-value is half the observed bin plus everything more extreme rather than the cumulative distribution, because the cumulative form gives a p-value of one in the most extreme case and no usable Z.

cases.why: From the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner. 69 test results and 162 Z scores, bit-identical on the first run, which covers both regimes: the permutation test at nine and nine, the normal approximation one element later, and the float rank sums at three hundred a side where single precision stops being exact.

suites.title: BaseQRankSum, MQRankSum, ReadPosRankSum and ClippingRankSum
suites.why: The four rank-sum annotations run a Mann-Whitney U test of the alternate reads against the reference reads and report a Z score, and four things decide what a consumer sees. The alternate goes first, so swapping the two arrays would flip the sign of every value this family reports and nothing downstream would notice. The value is a String, formatted with a three-decimal format that rounds half up on the decimal expansion rather than however a Double would render, so the VCF carries text and not a number. A NaN Z score is not written at all, which means a site with no alternate reads has no MQRankSum field rather than one reading zero. And three filters run before a read contributes, one of which ReadPosRankSum overrides to add a soft-clip test against the variant's end plus one, so the four members do not see the same reads.

cases.why: From the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner. 56 answers, 21 of them an absent key rather than a value, and no corrections. The absent ones are what the suite is for: null likelihoods, no genotypes, an empty matrix, and a site whose alternate series is empty all produce no field at all rather than a field reading zero.

suites.title: FS, SOR and SB
suites.why: The three strand-bias annotations read one 2x2 contingency table three ways, and four things decide what a consumer sees. The table is built per sample and only then added up, and a sample under the threshold contributes nothing rather than contributing to a pooled total that would pass, with FS using a minimum count of two and SOR of zero, so the two do not see the same table. The genotype field wins: if any genotype carries SB, both are computed from those per-sample arrays and the likelihood matrix is never consulted, which makes SB load-bearing rather than diagnostic. FS normalises a table above four hundred reads by scaling to about two hundred and truncating to int, so a deep site is scored from a table that no longer sums to its coverage, while SOR does not normalise at all. And FS is phred-scaled off a floor of 1e-320, which exists to prevent infinities, so the largest value a site can report is about 3200 whatever the evidence. The p-value itself goes through Math.pow, which decision 0007 deferred, so this suite is also where the port learns whether the platform's pow agrees with the reference's on these inputs.

cases.why: From the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner. 87 rows, no corrections, and sixteen of them are Fisher p-values that pass through Math.pow(10, x). Decision 0007 deferred that function because its intrinsic is GPL2 and not correctly rounded; the port calls the platform's powf, and on every input these annotations produce the two agree bit for bit. That is evidence, not a proof: it extends the pow measurement of decision 0007 rather than closing it.

suites.title: AS_UNIQ_ALT_READ_COUNT, BQHIST and REF_BASES
suites.why: Three annotations whose output shape is more interesting than their arithmetic. AS_UNIQ_ALT_READ_COUNT counts distinct start and fragment-length pairs rather than reads, so a hundred PCR duplicates of one fragment count once and two genuinely different fragments sharing both numbers also count once, and the value is a String joined with a pipe because it is an allele-specific raw annotation. BQHIST is a flat list of one entry per distinct quality followed by one count per allele of the matrix in matrix order, so its length depends on the matrix rather than on the variant and reading it requires knowing that number. And REF_BASES is twenty-one bases taken out of whatever window the reference context carries, with the discard clamped at zero and the right end padded with N, so the string has a fixed length and is not necessarily centred on the variant.

cases.why: From the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner. 24 rows, no corrections. The three-duplicates row is the one that carries the claim: three reads, one fragment, one count.

suites.title: AD, AF, DP and the marginalisation under them
suites.why: AD, AF and the HaplotypeCaller's DP are all counted off a marginalised likelihood matrix, and the marginalisation's allele order is a HashMap's. Collectors.toMap builds one and marginalize takes its key set as the new allele array, so the order follows Allele.hashCode, which is the bases' array hash times thirty-one plus the boolean hash of the reference flag. That order is observable, because searchBestAllele breaks a tie by keeping the first index, so a read supporting two alleles equally is attributed to whichever the hash put first. marginalize itself takes the maximum likelihood of the old alleles a new one stands for rather than their sum. AD is keyed on the variant's alleles and counted over the matrix, so an allele the matrix holds and the variant does not is counted into a bucket nobody reads. AF drops the first entry, so it is one shorter than AD and the two do not line up by index. And DP counts informative reads only, so it can be lower than the INFO-level DP over the same site.

cases.why: From the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner. 41 rows. The order rows are the point: A*,C comes out C,A* and A*,C,G,T comes out T,C,A*,G, so the marginalised matrix does not follow the variant's allele order. The golden corrected the port on one thing, normalizeSumToOne, which has no zero guard: an all-zero AD divides zero by zero, so a site with no informative reads gets an AF of NaN rather than of zero. Two of those rows are an invalid operation's NaN whose sign is the FPU's, exempted off x86-64 under decision 0012.

suites.title: The eight flow-based annotations
suites.why: The flow annotations describe a variant in flow space rather than in base space, and the encoding is where their surprises are. A flow key is a run-length encoding against a repeating flow order, TGCA by default, and N matches every flow base, so an ambiguous base is absorbed into whatever run it sits in rather than breaking it; a base the order does not contain trips a period guard and throws. An hmer indel is one whose reference and alternate flow keys differ in exactly one flow, with the length reported being the larger of the two and the nucleotide the order's base at that index, so a second differing flow disqualifies the site entirely. VARIANT_TYPE asks three questions in order and one ordinary indel beside an hmer one makes the whole site non-h-indel. A motif that would run off the contig is not truncated but dropped, so the annotation is absent rather than short. The left motif shifts for an indel, dropping its first base and appending the reference's first, so the two motifs of a mixed site come from different windows. And GC_CONTENT is a float rather than a double, so it carries single precision into the VCF.

cases.why: From the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner. 117 rows, and the golden corrected the port on four points, all of them about what happens at the edge of a reference window. A symbolic allele has length zero rather than the length of its text, so <NON_REF> classifies as a deletion. The two motifs are written into the attribute map independently, so a left motif that ran off the window leaves the right one in place. CycleSkipStatus declares that an actual flow order is required and therefore normally produces nothing, but it dereferences the motif lists before that check, so it throws a NullPointerException where the left motif is missing. And where the right motif's attribute was not written but its list survives with nulls in it, Java concatenates the four characters null into the sequence, whose characters are not bases, so the flow key's period guard trips and the exception is a GATKException instead.

suites.title: QD, the genotype summaries and LikelihoodRankSum
suites.why: QD above thirty-five is randomised: the reference replaces it with thirty plus a Gaussian jitter, so the value written to a VCF is a draw from a seeded generator rather than a function of the data. The port refuses that branch instead of approximating it, because nextGaussian goes through StrictMath.log, which is fdlibm and differs from the correctly-rounded logarithm this programme has on 186 of the corpus's 44,996 points. The suite therefore measures where the boundary is and what the raw ratio was, not what lies past it. The depth QD divides by is also not DP: only het and hom-var genotypes count, the whole AD total is added for each, and a separate AD-restricted tally collects the same totals only where the alternate part exceeds one, and if that tally ends non-zero it replaces the depth entirely, so one sample with two alternate reads can discard every other sample's depth. GQ_MEAN and GQ_STDDEV are strings and the deviation is written only with more than one GQ. NCC counts no-call alleles rather than no-call samples. And LikelihoodRankSumTest is the one member of the rank-sum family whose value comes from the matrix rather than from the read.

cases.why: From the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner. 30 rows, of which two are QD values the reference randomised: the suite asserts that the port refuses exactly those, that the raw ratio really was at or past thirty-five, and that what the reference wrote is not the ratio. The golden corrected the port on one point: getNoCallCount counts no-call genotypes rather than the no-call alleles inside them, so a diploid no-call sample contributes one and not two.

suites.title: ExcessHet, InbreedingCoeff, MQ, MQ0 and the tandem repeats
suites.why: ExcessHet and InbreedingCoeff ask the same question of a cohort and answer it from the same three numbers, computed by one function called with opposite rounding flags, so the two annotations on one site can disagree about how many hets there are and both are right. The rounded branch guards against counting a genotype twice by comparing two normalised likelihoods for exact floating-point equality, which is reachable from PLs of [0,0,X] and [X,0,0], and a hom-ref genotype with no likelihoods at all is given a distribution invented from its GQ in three different ways. ExcessHet saturates below a p-value of 10e-60, which is 1e-59 and not 1e-60, so values above the saturating 160.0000 do occur. MQ drops reads whose mapping quality is 255 from both the numerator and the denominator, so an all-unavailable matrix divides by zero and the annotation is the four characters NaN, while MQ0 answers zero for an empty matrix where every other annotation in this crate answers nothing. And findRepeatedSubstring cannot see a partial trailing repeat, because Arrays.copyOfRange pads with zero bytes past the end of the array and a zero byte is not a base.

cases.why: From the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner. 128 rows: 40 genotype-count triples compared as raw bits, 40 cohort annotations, 27 mapping-quality answers and 21 repeat measurements. The counts are bits rather than decimals because they are what the two annotations divide and index by, and the first candidate golden earned that choice: it caught the port calling MathUtils.log10sumLog10 where normalizeLog10 calls log10SumLog10, one letter apart and two ulp apart, on the equilibrium cohort's het count and on nothing else.

suites.title: The three allele-specific rank sums, and the histogram they travel as
suites.why: The direct annotate() path of an allele-specific annotation is not allele-specific: it pools every alternate's reads into one series and reports one Z score, exactly as its non-allele-specific parent does, under a different key. The allele-specific part lives entirely in the raw gVCF path, where the raw string starts with its delimiter because the reference allele is skipped but its slot is not, and the parser reads the slots positionally, so a raw string whose leading delimiter were trimmed would shift every allele by one. A site with no unambiguous reference read produces a string of bare delimiters rather than a missing value per allele. And each Z score is stored as a one-entry histogram binned to a tenth by a floor, so a negative score bins away from zero, the binning is not symmetric about it, and the joint-called AS_MQRankSum is the median of those bins rather than the rank sum of the pooled reads.

cases.why: From the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner. 100 rows: 11 histograms, 5 compressed lists, 16 binnings one value at a time, 27 direct and 27 raw allele-specific answers, and 7 combinations with their finalisations. The binning rows are what make the claim that a negative score bins away from zero a measurement rather than a reading of the source, and the ref-only row is what showed that a site with reference reads and no alternate read writes the four characters NaN into the raw field: the rank sum of an empty series is NaN, Histogram.add drops it, and an empty histogram renders as Double.toString(Double.NaN).

suites.title: AS_FS, AS_SOR and the strand table they share
suites.why: AS_SB_TABLE writes an entry for the reference too and puts the delimiter between entries, so it does not start with one, while the allele-specific rank sums skip the reference's value but keep its slot and theirs does: two families, two conventions for the same delimiter, and this parser refuses a count mismatch outright where the other pads. A sample contributes nothing at all unless its whole table holds more than two informative reads, so a sample with exactly two is dropped even for the allele that had both of them. AS_StrandOddsRatio computes a value for the reference allele against itself and then never prints it, while AS_FisherStrand filters the reference out first, and the two siblings differ in exactly that line. AS_FS floors its p-value at 1e-320, which is a subnormal, before phred-scaling it. And a reduced string skips an alternate the annotation data does not carry rather than writing the missing value, so the field can come out with fewer entries than the variant has alternates.

The golden corrected the port twice. An entry that is present but empty is not the same as an absent one: the combined field reads 10,8| with nothing after the delimiter, where the port had written 0,0. And the allele-specific minimum count is two for both members, while the plain StrandOddsRatio uses zero, so SOR and AS_SOR disagree on a site whose only sample has one or two informative reads.

suites.title: AS_QD, AS_MQ, AS_InbreedingCoeff and the heterozygosity calculator
suites.why: AS_QD has no raw data of its own: annotateRawData returns an empty map, its raw key is expected to be written by GenotypeGVCFs, and annotate is finalizeRawData with the same variant context passed twice. It adds the reference depth to every alternate's denominator, so a triallelic site's denominators overlap and the entries sum to nothing meaningful, and it inherits fixTooHighQD once per alternate, so one entry of a comma-separated field can be deterministic and the next drawn from a random generator. AS_MQ divides a sum of squares taken from the likelihood matrix by an AD summed from the genotypes, with nothing checking that the two describe the same reads, and its depth counts every genotype where AS_QD's counts only het and hom-var genotypes whose alternate depth exceeds one. AS_InbreedingCoeff is the only member that is not reducible and does not inherit from its non-allele-specific sibling, and its heterozygosity calculator adds the hom-ref mass to the reference's count once per alternate allele, so a triallelic site counts it twice.

The golden corrected the port twice. And AS_RMSMappingQuality collects into a bare ReducibleAnnotationData that nothing pre-populates, so an allele with no informative read has no key and is skipped entirely, while the parsed form is pre-populated with nulls and writes the missing value for the same state.

suites.title: The de novo calls and the transmitted singletons
suites.why: TransmittedSingleton reads the child's depth three times and names the three results childIsHighDepth, momIsHighDepth and dadIsHighDepth, so the parents' depths are never looked at and the annotation's own documented caveat about all three samples being deep is not what the code does. Genotype.getDP is minus one when absent rather than zero, and PossibleDeNovo's depth threshold defaults to zero, so a trio with no DP fails the high-confidence branch and falls into the low one, which does not test depth at all. isViolation indexes the child's alleles at zero and one and asks each parent to contain one of them rather than to be able to transmit it, so a half-called parent transmits whatever it does carry and only an entirely uncalled one reaches the special branches above. The de novo allele-frequency cutoff is the larger of a flat four samples and a thousandth of the cohort, so the flat four wins below four thousand samples. And the call-rate gate counts genotypes whose GQ is strictly greater than twenty where every other threshold in the pair is greater-or-equal.

suites.title: F1R2, F2R1, FAD and the fragment grouping under them
suites.why: groupEvidence sums the log likelihoods of a group rather than averaging them, so a pair whose reads each support an allele at minus one gives the fragment a minus two and the informativeness threshold, which is an absolute difference, is easier to clear after grouping than before. The new evidence order is a HashMap's over the read names, because groupingBy builds one. The pair's orientation, its usability and its base quality are all read off the first read of the fragment, which is the first in the sample's own order, so which read is consulted depends on the order the reads were added and a pair whose second read is poor is still counted. isF2R1 is isReverseStrand equals isFirstOfPair, and an unpaired read has isFirstOfPair false, so a forward unpaired read lands in F2R1 and a reverse one in F1R2, the opposite of what the names suggest. And the counts are keyed on the matrix's alleles and read back by the variant's, so an allele the variant declares and the matrix does not is a NullPointerException rather than a zero.

The trimming applies to the evidence object and not to the arithmetic.

suites.title: HaplotypeFilteringAnnotation: ASSEMBLED_HAPS and FILTERED_HAPS
suites.why: The fifty-second annotation, and the first JumboInfoAnnotation: it is handed three likelihood matrices and reads only the third, whose allele axis is a Haplotype rather than an Allele. That is what it was waiting on, not jmath. ASSEMBLED_HAPS is alleles().size() over an IndexedSet under Haplotype.equals, which compares the uniqueness value, the reference flag and the bases while Haplotype.hashCode compares the bases alone, so two haplotypes with identical bases are one entry or two depending on a field that never appears in the output; the duplicate-bases-same-uniqueness and duplicate-bases-different-uniqueness pair is what pins it. FILTERED_HAPS is a getter over an int field that only AlleleFiltering.subsetHaplotypesByAlleles ever writes, so a matrix nobody filtered reports zero rather than no key at all, and the getter does not clamp a value that exceeds the haplotypes remaining or a negative one. Neither key is ever guarded: the method has no branch. And the engine chooses between an AlleleLikelihoods over Fragment and one over GATKRead with a ternary, a difference Java erases behind a wildcard, so both branches are run over the same haplotypes and compared.

suites.title: The multi-pass walkers, and what they do between passes
suites.why: The last unported walkers of G1.6. Every other walker makes one traversal; these make several, and the three things they do between passes are each invisible from a single-pass run. MultiplePassVariantWalker builds one CountingVariantFilter and one CountingReadFilter before the loop and reuses both, so the filtered counts accumulate: the same file and the same predicate report one drop after a one-pass run, two after two passes and three after three. MultiplePassReadWalker builds a new filter at the top of every pass after the first and resets the reads data source, so each pass reports only its own drops; the two classes are one directory apart and disagree. afterNthPass is called inside the loop, so it runs after every pass including the last, which its own javadoc contradicts. TwoPassVariantWalker routes afterNthPass(0) to afterFirstPass and guards with else-if n greater than one, so n equal to one matches neither branch and the call after the second pass does nothing at all: there is no afterSecondPass and no error either. And zero passes is a legal traversal that visits nothing, calls afterNthPass never, and still builds both filters.

suites.title: Barclay's argument value model
suites.why: G1.8's first slice: the layer a covering-array vector is interpreted by, run at library level with no tool around it. Six of its rules are not what the annotation names suggest. optional() does not decide whether an argument is optional: isOptional is the annotation OR a default that renders as something other than the string null, and an empty collection renders as null, so an initialised-but-empty List is required while an initialised-and-non-empty one is not. The string null is a value with three outcomes: it clears a collection, it throws on a non-optional argument, and it throws a different exception on a scalar whose raw field is primitive, which is a different question from the boxed class the range check asks. isValueOutOfRange begins with value equals null, so a null on a bounded numeric argument is an out-of-range error rather than an accepted null, and the message formats the bounds as integers only when the value is an Integer, so the same argument reports allowed range [1, 10] for a rejected zero and allowed range [1.0, 10.0] for a rejected null. checkArgumentRange tests the recommended range with that same method, which compares against the hard bounds, so the recommended-range warning can fire only for a null and is otherwise unreachable. A scalar refuses a second occurrence rather than taking the last one. And the grammar is jopt-simple's rather than Barclay's: the equals spelling is refused outright, a flag consumes a following token only when StrictBooleanConverter accepts it so --flag maybe leaves maybe as a positional argument, and the positional error message is built with Collectors.joining passed a delimiter where a prefix belongs, so one stray value renders as ',maybe}'.

The pair that carries the claim is bounded-below against bounded-null: the same argument and the same bounds, reported as allowed range [1, 10] and as allowed range [1.0, 10.0], because the formatter asks whether the value is an Integer and a null is not.

suites.title: Barclay's tagged arguments and collection-file expansion
suites.why: G1.8's second slice, and the two mechanisms a covering-array vector reaches as soon as it names a logical name or a file. Tags are rewritten before jopt-simple sees the command line: the option name is peeled off, the pair of tag and raw value is stored under a surrogate key built from the option string and the value, and the parser is handed the bare option name and that key. The key doing double duty as a uniqueness test is what makes the same option with the same tag and the same value twice a duplicate on the command line rather than two values, while the same tag with two different values is fine. A tag on a field whose type does not implement TaggedArgument is refused when the value is set rather than when it is parsed, and the message is built from getShortName plus a slash plus getFullName with no guard, so an argument with no short name reports itself as slash plain-scalar. The malformed forms are four different exception shapes and two of them name no argument at all, leaving two spaces in the message. Expansion is collection-only: a collection value ending in .list or .args becomes the file's lines, trimmed, without blanks or hash comments, while the identical value on a scalar stays a path and suppressFileExpansion turns it off; a tag on a collection whose value is an expansion file is written onto every value the file produced.

The pair that carries the claim is same-option-tag-and-value-twice against same-tag-different-values: the surrogate key is built from the option string and the value, so the first collides with itself and the second does not.

suites.title: Barclay's @ArgumentCollection flattening
suites.why: G1.8's third slice, and the mechanism by which -L, -XL and the read-filter arguments actually reach a tool: they are not declared on the tool at all, they live on collection objects it holds, and createArgumentDefinitions recurses into those and adds their fields to one flat namespace where nothing records which object an argument came from. Two orderings are decided there and neither is stated anywhere. getAllFields adds a class's own declared fields and then climbs to its superclass, so a subclass's fields are registered before the ones it inherits, and that order is the order values are propagated in and the order a missing required argument is reported in: a user who omits both a subclass's required argument and its base class's is told about the subclass's. And the recursion is depth-first at the position of the field, so a collection declared between two arguments splices its own arguments between them rather than appending them. Two more refusals happen while the definitions are built rather than while a command line is parsed: an ArgumentCollection field left null, and a field carrying both annotations. A duplicate alias is a third, and it is a construction failure rather than a shadowing rule, so an outer object and a nested one declaring the same name make the tool unusable before it sees an argument.

The rows that carry the claim are the eight defs rows: the subclass's own field is index 0, its nested collection occupies 1 to 4, and the base class's two fields are 6 and 7.

suites.title: Barclay's --arguments_file
suites.why: G1.8's fourth slice, and the only argument that changes the command line rather than a field. When the special arguments-file argument is present, parseArguments reads the named files, splits every non-comment non-blank line on runs of whitespace, and calls itself again on the result. The file's arguments come first, because newArgs.addAll(Arrays.asList(args)) appends the original command line to the expansion rather than the other way round, and it does so wherever the arguments-file argument itself sat: a collection given a value in a file and another on the command line ends up with the file's first either way, and a scalar given in both is cannot be specified more than once rather than an override. The recursion is bounded by a set of file names rather than a depth, and every file named in a pass goes into that set including ones skipped for already being there, so a file that includes itself is read once and two files that include each other are read once each. The argument is not removed from the command line between passes: the recursion terminates because the second expansion is empty, not because the argument is gone. And the tag surrogates are reset between passes, because the first pass built keys the second would build again. Splitting is StringUtils.split, which collapses runs of whitespace, so an argument value containing a space cannot be written in one of these files at all.

The pair that carries the claim is file-then-command-line against command-line-then-file: the same three values in the same order both ways, because the expansion is what the original command line is appended to.

suites.title: Barclay's plugin descriptors
suites.why: G1.8's fifth slice, measured through GATK's own GATKReadFilterPluginDescriptor over GATK's own read filters rather than a stand-in, because --read-filter is this mechanism. A descriptor names a base class and a package, ClassFinder finds every implementation, and each one's arguments are registered as controlled by that descriptor, so every read filter's arguments are in the parser on every run whether or not anybody asked for that filter. What decides whether one is usable is validatePluginArgumentValues, which runs before the required check and rewrites the list it checks: a controlled argument that nobody set and whose filter nobody named is removed from the list rather than treated as optional, so a required argument of an unselected filter would not fire at all. The same argument set without its filter is an error that names the filter class rather than --read-filter, and builds the argument's own name from the short name, a slash and the long name with no guard, so one with no short name reports a leading slash. And the refusal of a name matching no filter is the descriptor's own validateAndResolvePlugins rather than the argument layer, which is why its wording is GATK's.

The rows that carry the claim are no-filter against dependent-without-filter: the same argument, left alone and set, with an unselected filter.

suites.title: NaturalLogUtils, and the rows that cannot depend on exp
suites.why: G1.9.1, and the layer AllelePseudoDepth stands on. Compared as raw bit patterns, because the question is whether a port built on a permissively-licensed exp lands on the same double and decimal rendering discards exactly that. The reference calls Math.exp; the port calls FDLIBM, measured at one ulp worst case against it by htsjdk-rs decision 0025, so this suite is not a bit-identity claim and does not pretend to be. It separates three things. First, the rows that reach neither exp nor log and are therefore exact by construction: logSumExp starts its accumulator at one rather than zero because the maximum's own term is skipped in the loop and folded in as that one, and the guard sum not equal to one then skips the log entirely, so a single non-infinite entry, a maximum with everything else at negative infinity, and a difference large enough that one plus exp of it rounds back to one all return the maximum untouched. Second, the rows that do call exp, which must land within one ulp, and the test reports the worst distance rather than only passing. Third, the refusal, which fires on the accumulator after the loop rather than on the inputs, so a NaN input reaches it and a negative infinity input does not, though the message names the inputs either way. A row diverging by more than one ulp means the port's arithmetic is wrong rather than that the exponential is approximate, which is the distinction the suite is built to make.

cases.why: From the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner, published as the golden-pending artefact of the run that added this suite. 42 rows, no corrections. It happens to be byte-identical to an Apple Silicon run, which says the two hosts' Math.exp agreed on these particular inputs and says nothing about the general case; the provenance is what makes it a golden.

suites.title: The Dirichlet fixed point, with its iteration count
suites.why: G1.9.2. The variational fixed point AllelePseudoDepth ends in, and where G1.9's open question lives. G1.9.1 established that a one-ulp exp is what enters here; this measures what the iteration does with it, and there are two ways that could go wrong which look identical unless they are separated. Amplification, where the difference grows across iterations. And a different iteration count, because convergence is a threshold test on distance1 over sum against a thousandth, so a difference far too small to see in the values can still put one side of that comparison on the other side of the threshold, after which the two runs do a different amount of work. The second would be far larger than the first, so the golden carries the count and the suite asserts it exactly, before comparing any value. The count is not exposed by the engine, so the harness replays the loop body with the same calls in the same order and checks its replay against the engine's own answer on every case, which the agree rows record. The weights rows are the control: effectiveLogMultinomialWeights is digamma arithmetic with no exp in it, so they carry no bound and must be bit-identical.

cases.why: From the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner, published as the golden-pending artefact of the run that added this suite. 29 rows, no corrections. The result it carries is the one G1.9 needed: every iteration count matches and the worst value divergence is zero, so the fixed point neither amplifies the exp difference nor crosses its convergence threshold differently.

suites.title: DecimalFormat, for the two patterns AllelePseudoDepth emits through
suites.why: G1.9.3. AllelePseudoDepth writes strings, not numbers, so java.text.DecimalFormat is part of its output. The Javadoc specifies HALF_EVEN and the pattern language and says nothing about the three facts that decide printed digits, each established here by measurement rather than by reading the class, which is GPL2 and may not be transcribed. First, it rounds the SHORTEST decimal form and not the value: formatting 0.1 to forty places gives 0.1 rather than the double's true 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827. Second, an apparent tie is settled by which side of the halfway point the double sits on, so 0.155 rounds down and 0.165 rounds up although the digit strings are the same shape, and only when the shortest form IS the value is it a real tie for HALF_EVEN to break on parity. Third, the two patterns disagree with each other at one place: where the rounding position falls before the first digit, #.## follows the value and #.#### rounds to even, so 0.005 and 5e-5 are the same shape one decade apart and go opposite ways. Values are bit patterns because a decimal literal in a golden would be re-parsed into a possibly different double, which for a suite about the last digit is the whole question.

cases.why: From the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner, published as the golden-pending artefact of the run that added this suite. 315 rows, no corrections, and byte-identical to the same container on Apple Silicon: nothing the formatter does here depends on the host. 630 strings compared and two values diverge, both above 2^53, where Java 17's pre-Schubfach digit generation stops producing the shortest decimal form. Below that line there is no divergence at all, measured on 903,121 values.

suites.title: DD and DF, the annotation G1.9 was opened for
suites.why: G1.9.3, and the end of G1.9. AllelePseudoDepth emits its two keys as STRINGS through DecimalFormat at two and four decimals, which is what makes an oracle-backed suite possible at all for a chain that calls Math.exp: G1.9.1 measured the port within 1 ulp of the reference and G1.9.2 measured the fixed point at zero ulp, and the formatter is about twelve orders of magnitude coarser than a last bit. The suite therefore compares the formatted strings, which is the only thing the reference writes. Four behaviours are the reason for the case list, and none of them is the arithmetic. composePriorPseudoCounts memoises one array per allele count and hands out that array rather than a copy, so on the empty-evidence branch the posteriors ARE the memo and the closing subtraction zeroes it; every case is annotated twice with the same object, and the reference's own second answer for empty-evidence is NaN,NaN. The log10 branch's visitor receives (row, column) as (allele, read) and looks the mapping quality up at evidence().get(row), so a site with more alleles than reads throws IndexOutOfBoundsException and one with fewer floors each allele's row using an unrelated read's quality. The decay rate selects which intrinsics run: one Math.pow per read at the default, two when it is neither zero nor one, and none at zero, where the weights are null. And the guards put no key in the genotype at all, which is not the same as an empty one. The matrices are graded rather than symmetric, because a symmetric site gives every read the same weight and every setting of weightDecay the same answer.

All 46 calls match, including the two whose second answer differs from their first because the reference wrote through its own memo.

suites.title: CountBases, CountReads and FlagStat, whose output is a number rather than a BAM
suites.why: The first three tools whose output is a NUMBER rather than a BAM. All three are `ReadWalker`s whose `apply` is one line and whose whole answer is what `onTraversalSuccess` prints, so what they measure is the traversal and the formatting rather than any transform. THEIR DEFAULT FILTER IS THE ENGINE'S, WellformedReadFilter, so a malformed read is not counted by any of the three: a file holding nothing but two reads whose cigars disagree with their lengths counts 0, and 2 with the filter disabled. CountBases COUNTS read.getLength(), the number of BASES AND NOT THE SPAN, so twelve ten-base reads come to 120 whether they carry a deletion or an insertion. FlagStat's PERCENTAGES ARE COMPUTED IN float AND FORMATTED WITH DecimalFormat("#0.00"), which rounds HALF_EVEN where String.format("%.2f") rounds HALF_UP: two different roundings, and this is the one that reaches the output, 11 of 12 mapped coming out 91.67%. WITH NO READS AT ALL THE RATIO IS 0f/0f, so the percentage is NaN% , a real line of a real output and not an error. read2 IS TESTED BEFORE read1 AND THE TWO ARE `else if`, so a read carrying both 0x40 and 0x80 counts as read2 only. `singletons` AND `with_itself_and_mate_mapped` ARE BOTH INSIDE the paired branch, so an unpaired read contributes to neither however it is mapped. AND isUnmapped IS THE THREE-PART TEST rather than the 0x4 flag.

cases.why: 30 rows: three fixtures with their indexes, and eight runs of each. The corpus covers every branch of FlagStat's counter, an empty file where the percentages divide by zero, and a file holding only reads the default filter drops. Each fixture is run whole, over an interval that keeps half of it, and with WellformedReadFilter disabled. From the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner, published as the golden-pending artefact of run 31592539751, and byte for byte what an Apple Silicon laptop produced.

suites.title: SATagBuilder, the SA tag a split read carries
suites.why: The first piece of SplitNCigarReads, whose `repairSupplementaryTags` marks every piece after the first as supplementary and calls `setReadsAsSupplemental`. A UNIT IS SIX FIELDS SPLIT WITH `split(",", -1)`, so `chr1,100,+,10M,60,;` parses with an empty NM where the zero-limit split would have dropped the field and refused it. THE THREE VALIDATIONS ARE POS, CIGAR AND MAPQ, each accepting `*`; NM IS NOT VALIDATED AT ALL, so `not-a-number` round trips. THE STRAND IS NORMALISED ON THE WAY OUT, the one field that does not survive a round trip. A UNIT BUILT FROM AN UNMAPPED READ IS `*,0,+,*,0,*;`, where the position and the mapping quality are the read's own zeroes and not `toString`'s defaults, which no read can reach. addTag PUTS A NON-SUPPLEMENTARY READ AT THE FRONT, and setReadsAsSupplemental MARKS EVERY READ BUT THE FIRST BEFORE BUILDING ANY TAG, so the primary is the first unit of every tag. EXISTING SA TAGS ARE PRESERVED AND STAY FIRST. THE PRIMARY IS NEVER UN-MARKED, so a family whose primary arrives with 0x800 comes out with no primary line at all. AND A FAMILY OF ONE WRITES NOTHING, because `setSATag` on an empty builder leaves the read alone rather than giving it an empty tag.

From the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner, published as the golden-pending artefact of run 31597074001, and byte for byte what an Apple Silicon laptop produced.

suites.title: OverhangFixingManager, the overhang clipper SplitNCigarReads writes through
suites.why: The second piece of SplitNCigarReads, and the one that decides what the output reads look like. overhangingBasesMismatch REFUSES THREE KINDS OF SPAN BEFORE COUNTING ANYTHING: below 1, above --max-bases-in-overhang, and STRICTLY LONGER than half the read's non-clipped length, where the division is integer and the comparison is `>`, so on ten bases a span of five is tested and six is refused while on NINE bases five is already refused. IT HAS TWO WAYS TO SAY YES: the tolerance, and a span where at least (span+1)/2 bases mismatch, so one mismatch out of two is a mismatch although the tolerance is one. isLeftOverhang AND isRightOverhang MIX STRICT AND NON-STRICT COMPARISONS, so a read starting exactly at the splice start is neither and one starting a base later is a left overhang. addSplicePosition RETURNS null BOTH FOR A SPLICE ALREADY HELD AND FOR A MANAGER WITH FIXING TURNED OFF, told apart only by what is held afterwards, and A SPLICE ON A NEW CONTIG CLEARS EVERYTHING SEEN SO FAR. THE QUEUE FLUSHES HALFWAY UNDER PRESSURE and completely on a new contig. THE FAMILY IS REPAIRED ON THE WAY OUT, NM, MD and NH cleared and the SA tags written, and only when writing is active. A SECONDARY ALIGNMENT IS WRITTEN BUT NOT CLIPPED unless --process-secondary-alignments is given. activateWriting A SECOND TIME IS A GATKException. AND THE MATE KEY IS name@0-or-1@start, whose digit is !isFirstOfPair when stored and isFirstOfPair when looked up, carrying the read's OLD start, so a mate already pointing at the clipped read's new position misses.

The two protected predicates and the package-private key builder are reached by reflection. From the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner, published as the golden-pending artefact of run 31598493960, and byte for byte what an Apple Silicon laptop produced.

suites.title: SplitNCigarReads, the RNA-seq splitter the last two suites were built for
suites.why: The thirteenth whole tool of the record-transform archetype, and the first that is a MultiplePassReadWalker: the input is traversed TWICE, the first pass recording which reads the overhang clipper moved and the second writing them out with their mates repaired. A READ WITH k N ELEMENTS BECOMES k+1 READS, each keeping every base and soft clipping the rest, so 3M2N5M comes out 3M5S and 3S5M. A SECTION BESIDE A DELETION IS TRIMMED BEFORE THE CLIP, and N-D-N is an IllegalArgumentException naming the cigar unless --refactor-cigar-string merges the motif into one N first; the refactor merges ONE motif per two elements skipped, so 3M2N1D2N1D2N2M comes out 3M5N1D2N2M. A CIGAR ENDING IN N EMITS ONE PIECE AND LOSES THE N; A CIGAR BEGINNING WITH N IS PASSED THROUGH UNTOUCHED. THE MAPPING QUALITY TRANSFORM REWRITES 255 AND ONLY 255, to 60, unless skipped. ITS DEFAULT FILTER IS ALLOW_ALL_READS, so a malformed read is still written. AN MC TAG IS REWRITTEN to what the mate's cigar will become, computed by splitting an artificial read carrying it. A SECONDARY ALIGNMENT IS NOT SPLIT unless --process-secondary-alignments is given. suites.title: SAMPileupCodec, the samtools mpileup format CheckPileup reads as its truth
suites.why: THE FIELD COUNT MUST BE 4 TO 6, WHICH IS NOT THE FORMAT'S. THE BASES COLUMN IS A LITTLE LANGUAGE: `.` and `,` are the reference base, `*` is a deletion, `$` ends a read and consumes NO quality, `^` eats the NEXT character as a mapping quality, and `+`/`-` skip an indel whose length is the number that follows. THE QUALITY STRING IS THEREFORE CONSUMED AT A DIFFERENT RATE FROM THE BASES STRING, which is why leftover qualities are their own error and leftover bases are unreachable. A DELETION BECOMES THE LETTER `D`, which is not a base the reads column itself would accept. A COVERAGE OF ZERO RETURNS EARLY, so a line whose bases and qualities are nonsense parses. TWO MESSAGES CARRY TYPOS a port has to carry too, "THe SAM pileup line" and "this codes is only valid". AN N FOLDS TO N and every other base comes out upper case. suites.title: The tsv table format, under every .table file GATK writes
suites.why: GATK's own table format and the first shared piece of CalculateContamination. METADATA IS A TAGGED COMMENT, `#<METADATA>key=value`: a hand-written `#sample=s1` looks like metadata and is a plain comment. AND THE MAP IS FILLED BY processCommentLine ITSELF, so a subclass that overrides that method without calling super LOSES EVERY PAIR; the same file read twice, once with an override and once without, gives an empty map and `sample=s1`. A VALUE IS QUOTED ONLY WHEN IT HAS TO BE: a space and a comma pass through bare, a tab, a quote and a backslash force quotes, and a value beginning with the comment prefix is written unquoted. THE ESCAPE IS THE BACKSLASH inside quotes. THE HEADER IS WRITTEN EVEN WITH NO RECORDS AND EVEN WHEN IT WAS NEVER ASKED FOR. A DOUBLE IS String.valueOf's SPELLING, so a third is 0.3333333333333333, 1e-7 is 1.0E-7 and the non-finite ones are NaN and Infinity. A ROW OF THE WRONG WIDTH IS THE SAME REFUSAL IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, naming the file, the line and both counts. A COLUMN THE HEADER LACKS IS A PLAIN IllegalArgumentException AND NOT A UserException. AND AN EMPTY NUMERIC FIELD ONLY FAILS WHEN IT IS ASKED FOR AS A NUMBER, with a message that names the column and ends in a space because the value is printed unquoted.
